561.title: Shurpanakha
561.hook: a visitor walks up to the hut at Panchavati and, within a minute, proposes marriage
561.carry: a joke can turn ugly fast
561.howItsDone: The Shurpanakha episode is a turning point in the Ramayana, and some modern writers, performers and commentators have revisited it from her side of the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: on a cold dawn walk, Rama stopped Lakshmana from blaming Kaikeyi. Speak only of Bharata.

The quiet ends the way a lot of trouble starts: with someone noticing someone. Rama sits outside the hut, talking with Sita and Lakshmana, when a rakshasi, a woman of the rakshasa people, comes through the trees and sees him. She stops. She wants him, right then, completely. She walks straight up and asks: who are you, dressed like a hermit but carrying a bow, with a wife beside you, in a forest that belongs to rakshasas?
screen: `SOMEONE NOTICES SOMEONE.` → `A RAKSHASI AT THE HUT.` → `WHO ARE YOU, WITH A BOW?`

segments.voice: Rama answers plainly: his name, his father's, Sita's and Lakshmana's, and why they're in the forest. Then he asks who she is. Her answer reshapes the story. I am Shurpanakha, she says, sister of Ravana, king of the rakshasas, and of Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana, and of Khara and Dushana, who rule this part of the forest. I saw you and I want you. Be my husband. Leave this woman. Then it turns ugly: she says she'll eat Sita, and Lakshmana too. Her name shows how Valmiki sees her. Shurpa is a winnowing basket, the wide flat tray for sifting grain; nakha is a fingernail. She of the nails like winnowing fans. Line by line, Valmiki describes her as everything Rama isn't. Rama's response is to laugh and joke. He tells her he's married and suggests she try his brother. Lakshmana jokes back: I'm only Rama's servant; you'd be a servant's wife. Go back to him. She goes back and forth between them, angrier each time. Here, honesty matters. Some readers have been uneasy with this scene: two princes teasing a woman whose feelings, however fierce, are real to her. Others read the teasing as a way to turn aside a dangerous moment without violence. The text doesn't stop to settle it. It hurries on, because her anger is about to become something much worse.

segments.voice: Think of a time someone laughed at you, or you laughed at someone, when it wasn't funny to the other person. Notice where it lands in your body, without judging anyone. Then breathe out slowly and let your face soften: the jaw, the eyes, the mouth.

562.title: Shurpanakha
562.hook: the joking stops when she lunges at Sita, and what follows will start a war
562.howItsDone: The mutilation of Shurpanakha is staged in Ramlila performances, and it is much discussed in modern Ramayana retellings and criticism.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's sister demanded Rama marry her, and the brothers answered with jokes. A joke can turn ugly fast.

Sent back and forth between the brothers, laughed at and refused, Shurpanakha turns on the person she blames. It's because of her, she says, looking at Sita. I'll eat her right now, and then you'll be mine. She rushes at Sita, and Valmiki compares it to a great meteor hurtling toward a gentle star. Sita, who has said nothing through all of this, is terrified. There's no more time for jokes.
screen: `SHE BLAMES SITA.` → `A METEOR AT A GENTLE STAR.` → `NO MORE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Rama catches her, holds her back, and speaks sharply to Lakshmana. We shouldn't joke with the cruel, he says. Look how close Sita came. Mark her, so she can't do this again. Lakshmana draws his sword and cuts off her nose and ears. Shurpanakha flees screaming into the forest, bleeding, to her brother Khara at Janasthana. It's a violent scene, and hard to sit with. Some devotional readers see it simply: a rakshasi tried to kill Sita, and the brothers stopped her without taking her life. Others, especially modern readers, find the punishment harsh, all the more after the teasing. Tellings differ, too. In some later versions, like Kamban's Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas, she first appears in a beautiful disguise, which changes how the scene feels. In recent decades, writers have retold it from Shurpanakha's own side: rejected, mocked, wounded. There's no single reading everyone shares, and it's fine to hold the discomfort. What the text makes plain is that this is a hinge. Her wound goes first to Khara, and from Khara the story will travel to Lanka, to Ravana. A rejected proposal at a hut by a river leads, step by step, to Sita's abduction and a war: a disaster that starts small, with hurt and pride on more than one side.

563.title: Khara and Dushana
563.hook: a wounded sister reaches her brother's court, and an army of fourteen thousand gets ready to march
563.howItsDone: Valmiki lingers over the omens before the battle at Janasthana, and Rama's choice to send Sita and Lakshmana to safety is a familiar scene in performances.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha lunged at Sita, Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears, and she fled to Khara. A disaster that starts small.

Shurpanakha falls at her brother's feet, covered in blood. Khara rules Janasthana, the rakshasa stronghold in Dandaka, with his general Dushana. He's furious and proud, and both show. Who did this to you? Tell me, and I'll drink their blood. She tells him: two young men in bark clothes, with bows, and a woman. Khara's first move is almost casual. He sends fourteen rakshasas to kill them, and to bring their blood back for his sister.
screen: `AT KHARA'S FEET.` → `WHO DID THIS?` → `FOURTEEN SENT TO KILL.`

segments.voice: The fourteen reach Panchavati with Shurpanakha pointing the way. Rama asks Lakshmana to stay by Sita and speaks to them first. We live here as hermits, at the sages' request. If you've come to fight, stop where you are. They don't. They hurl their spears, and Rama's arrows cut down all fourteen. Shurpanakha runs back to Khara screaming, and this time she shames him. You call yourself a warrior, and you sent fourteen? Now Khara is truly enraged. He calls up his whole force: fourteen thousand rakshasas, with Dushana and Trishiras, the three-headed. As they march, Valmiki piles up the omens: a rain of blood, jackals howling, the sun dimmed, Khara's left arm throbbing. Khara ignores every one. At the hut, Rama sees signs too, and reads them. Then he does something unexpected. He tells Lakshmana to take Sita to a cave in the mountain, hidden by trees, and stay with her there. I'll face them alone, he says. Lakshmana could argue. He doesn't. He takes his bow and Sita and goes. A small attack, a humiliation, an overwhelming answer, and a man who stands in front of it by himself, so the people he loves are out of reach.

564.title: Khara and Dushana
564.hook: the sages and the gods gather in the sky to watch one man stand in front of an army
564.howItsDone: The battle of Janasthana is told in many Ramlila performances, and devotees often point to it as the moment Rama's promise to the forest sages is fulfilled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen thousand marched, and Rama sent Sita and Lakshmana to a cave. I'll face them alone.

Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and waits outside the empty hut. Valmiki says the sages, the gods and the celestial beings gather in the sky above Janasthana to watch. Some are worried: one man against fourteen thousand. They pray for him aloud. Then dust rises on the horizon, the drums grow louder, and Khara's army comes into view, a dark mass like storm clouds rolling in.
screen: `ARMOR ON, BOW STRUNG.` → `THE GODS WATCH FROM THE SKY.` → `AN ARMY LIKE STORM CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells the battle over several chapters. Rama's arrows fly so fast, he says, that the rakshasas can't see him draw or release, only the bow bent into a circle. The army falls back, regroups, and charges again. Dushana leads one assault and falls. Trishiras, the three-headed, comes next, and falls too. Then only Khara is left, and their fight is fierce. Khara cuts Rama's bow and shatters his armor; Rama takes up another bow and goes on. Khara even tears up a tree and hurls it. They trade taunts, and Rama names what Khara has done: the sages terrorized, the hermits killed in the forest. At last Rama fits an arrow, and Khara falls. The text says it was over in a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour. The gods rain flowers, and the sages come down to praise him. Then Lakshmana brings Sita out of the cave, and Sita, seeing Rama alive and unhurt among grateful sages, runs and holds him. A few days ago, Rama promised the sages protection, and Sita asked whether that promise was wise. Today it's kept, at full cost, by one person. But one rakshasa, Valmiki says, slipped away. His name is Akampana, and he's heading south, toward the sea, toward Lanka.

565.title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
565.hook: the king of Lanka hears the news, makes a plan, and is talked out of it on the first try
565.carry: pride stung in public is harder to talk down
565.tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part two
565.howItsDone: Recitations of the Aranya Kanda that tell this part in full keep Maricha's first refusal, so listeners hear that Ravana was talked out of the plan once before Shurpanakha's scolding changed his mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama alone defeated Khara's army and kept his promise to the sages, but Akampana escaped. One escapes to Lanka.

Until now, the Ramayana has spoken of Ravana without showing him. Now the story crosses the sea, into his city. Akampana arrives in Lanka shaking and tells the king of the rakshasas everything: Janasthana is empty, Khara and Dushana are dead, fourteen thousand lie on the field, and one man did it. Ravana's first response is rage. Who is this man? I'll burn him. And Akampana says: you can't beat him. But I know how you can hurt him.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA, IN LANKA.` → `ONE MAN DID THIS.` → `I KNOW HOW TO HURT HIM.`

segments.voice: Akampana's idea is cold. Rama has a wife, Sita, and no woman in the world, he says, is her equal in beauty. Carry her off, and Rama will die of grief without a single arrow. Ravana likes it. He takes his chariot across the sea to an old acquaintance, Maricha, the rakshasa Rama spared years ago at Vishvamitra's sacrifice, hurling him out to sea alive. Maricha has lived as a kind of hermit since. Ravana asks for help, and Maricha says no. Whoever told you to do this, he says, is your enemy pretending to be your friend. Rama is a sleeping lion; don't go poke him. Go home, enjoy your wives, and let him live with his. And here's the surprise: Ravana listens, and goes home to Lanka. If the story stopped there, it would be about good advice taken. But Shurpanakha arrives at Ravana's court, mutilated, and she doesn't plead. She scolds. What kind of king are you, lost in pleasure while a man destroys your army and your frontier? You don't even know what's happening in your own lands. Then she describes Sita, at length. The warning that worked once is about to be overruled.

566.title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
566.hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare
566.carry: pleasant things are easy to find
566.tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part three
566.howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court. Pride stung in public is harder to talk down.

Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: shores lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and merchants' ships. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage a second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime; he went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit: ramo vigrahavan dharmah. Rama is dharma in bodily form: right living, duty and truth, with a body and a bow. To steal his wife is to walk into a fire. You'll ruin yourself, your city and your people. Look at who's speaking. Not a sage, not a god, not one of Rama's friends, but a rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, once hurled across the sea by him. He has met Rama as an enemy, and that gives his words their weight. He's using everything he knows to save his own king from himself.

567.title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
567.hook: an old rakshasa admits that he sees Rama behind every tree in the forest
567.carry: better to die by Rama's hand
567.howItsDone: Some Ramayana teachers use Maricha's confession, seeing Rama in every tree, as a striking example of how the mind dwells on what it fears, and some devotional readers see a strange kind of devotion in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha told his king the hard truth. Pleasant things are easy to find, and Rama is dharma in bodily form.

Maricha has given his king the argument. Now he gives him something more personal: his fear. Let me tell you how I know Rama, he says. I was strong once, and proud. I went to break up Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and a boy, barely grown, shot me with one arrow and threw me a hundred yojanas into the sea. I lived. And I didn't learn, not then. It took a second meeting.
screen: `NOT AN ARGUMENT: A FEAR.` → `A BOY WITH ONE ARROW.` → `INTO THE SEA, ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Later, Maricha says, I came into Dandaka with two others, all three of us in the shape of deer, eating sages. Rama saw us and shot three arrows. My two companions died. I ran. Since then I've given all that up and live as a hermit. But I can't get away from him. I see Rama in every tree, dressed in bark, holding his bow. I see him in my dreams. Even words that start with his sound, ratna, jewel, ratha, chariot, frighten me. It's an astonishing confession from a villain, and a very human one. Then Ravana answers, and you can hear how this was always going to end. I didn't come for advice. A king's minister speaks when asked. Do as I say, or I'll kill you now. Maricha sees the trap. If I go, Rama kills me. If I refuse, you kill me. So he chooses. Better to die at the hands of an enemy like Rama, he says, than by my own king. And he goes. Now the week. Shurpanakha at the hut, and the brothers' jokes. The attack on Sita, and the wound that started the war. Fourteen, then fourteen thousand, and Rama standing alone. Akampana's escape. Ravana talked out of it, then shamed into it. And Maricha's warning, the rarest kind of advice, refused.
